Press Play to watch \(A\) transform space. \(\vec{e}_1\), \(\vec{e}_2\) and \(\vec{e}_3\) are the unit vectors along the axes, and the unit cube is carried along with them: the three edges become the columns \(\vec{u}\), \(\vec{v}\) and \(\vec{w}\). The input \(\vec{x}=(1,0.5,1.5)\), which is \(1\vec{e}_1+0.5\vec{e}_2+1.5\vec{e}_3\), becomes \(1\vec{u}+0.5\vec{v}+1.5\vec{w}=\vec{b}\), the same vector as in Figure 1. That is why the two perspectives agree.



For any given input \(\vec{x}\), we can apply the matrix \(A\) and obtain the corresponding output \(\vec{b}\).
Actually, these two perspectives describe exactly the same mathematical operation.
One perspective treats matrix-vector multiplication as a linear combination of the columns of a matrix. The other treats it as a linear transformation applied to an input vector.
There is also a third way to read \(A\vec{x}\), and it is how we usually compute it by hand: each entry of \(\vec{b}\) is the dot product of one row of \(A\) with \(\vec{x}\). The second row of \(A\) is \((-1,1,0)\), and \((-1,1,0)\cdot(x_1,x_2,x_3)=x_2-x_1\), which is exactly the second entry of \(\vec{b}\). So the dot product from the previous post is hiding inside every matrix multiplication.
This is where I started to understand matrices from a geometric perspective: a matrix is not just a collection of numbers. It can also represent a linear transformation in space.

title: Matrices as Transformations
text:
2 Matrix as a Linear Transformation
If a matrix represents a linear transformation, a natural question arises: what actually happens to vectors in space after we apply this transformation?
Instead of considering a single vector, let’s consider an entire set of vectors.
Suppose our input vector \(\vec{x}\) can take any value in three-dimensional space. What kind of set will these vectors form after applying the matrix \(A\)?
Or let’s make the question more specific.
Suppose all input vectors are restricted to a three-dimensional unit ball:
\[
x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2\leq1
\]
What will happen to this ball after a linear transformation?
Could it be stretched into an ellipsoid? Could it be compressed onto a two-dimensional plane, becoming an elliptical disk? Could it even collapse into a line segment or a single point?
All of these are possible.1 Figure 3 shows the same idea one dimension lower, where the ball is a disk and its image is an ellipse, a line segment, or a single point.
1 What shapes can a linear transformation produce? My first idea was that a linear transformation could turn a ball into almost any shape, such as a cube or a rectangular box. When I explored this with AI, it pointed out that this is not possible: a ball under a linear transformation can only become an ellipsoid or one of its degenerate forms, such as an elliptical disk, a line segment, or a point. Turning a ball into a cube would need a nonlinear transformation. I haven’t studied why this restriction exists yet, so I’ll leave it for later.





  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  uv
  


  Identity
  Stretch
  Rotate
  Shear
  Project
  Dependent







Figure 3: A matrix in two dimensions. A matrix \(A\) with columns \(\vec{u}\) and \(\vec{v}\). Drag their tips or pick an example. The grid shows where the whole plane goes, the unit circle becomes the solid curve, and the shaded unit square becomes a parallelogram whose area is \(|\det A|\). When \(\vec{u}\) and \(\vec{v}\) point along the same line, the plane collapses onto that line.



I find this perspective particularly interesting. Instead of studying only how one vector changes, we can investigate how an entire set of vectors is transformed.
From this perspective, matrices can describe various linear transformations, such as stretching, compression, rotation, reflection, and projection.
We can also investigate which properties are preserved during these transformations, such as vector lengths, angles between vectors, and the dimension of the resulting space.

2.1 Some Examples of Linear Transformations
Let’s start with a simple example: the identity matrix.
\[
I=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
0&1&0\\
0&0&1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
For any vector:
\[
I\vec{x}=\vec{x}
\]
It does not change any coordinate of the input vector. Whatever the original vector is, it remains exactly the same after the transformation.
Now consider two other matrices:
\[
P_1=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
0&0&0\\
0&0&0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
P_2=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
0&1&0\\
0&0&0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Their transformations are:
\[
P_1
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
P_2
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\0\end{bmatrix}
\]
Figure 4 shows what these matrices do to the unit ball.













Figure 4: What each matrix does to the unit ball. The unit ball and the unit vectors \(\vec{e}_1\), \(\vec{e}_2\) and \(\vec{e}_3\) under the matrices of this section. Pick a matrix to watch the transformation, and drag the figure to rotate it.



The first matrix preserves only the \(x_1\) coordinate and removes the other two coordinates.
If the original input set is a three-dimensional ball, the transformed set will lie entirely on the \(x_1\)-axis, forming a line segment.
The second matrix preserves \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) but removes \(x_3\).
The same three-dimensional ball will become a disk on the \(x_1x_2\)-plane.
In other words, these matrices reduce the dimension of the original set and discard some information.
If we modify some entries of the matrix, for example changing one of the nonzero diagonal entries of \(P_2\) from 1 to 2, the resulting disk becomes an elliptical disk (the fourth example in Figure 4).
What if a matrix keeps all three coordinates but scales them by different amounts? For example:
\[
S=
\begin{bmatrix}
1.5&0&0\\
0&1&0\\
0&0&0.5
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Its transformation is:
\[
S
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}1.5x_1\\x_2\\0.5x_3\end{bmatrix}
\]
Pick \(S\) in Figure 4: the ball is stretched along the \(x_1\)-axis and squeezed along the \(x_3\)-axis, so it becomes an ellipsoid. Unlike \(P_1\) and \(P_2\), \(S\) does not remove any coordinate, so the result is still three-dimensional and no information is lost.
Now consider another matrix:
\[
R=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
0&0&-1\\
0&1&0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
It performs the following transformation:
\[
R\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\-x_3\\x_2\end{bmatrix}
\]
This transformation has an interesting property.
It does not change the length of the vector:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|R\vec{x}\|^2
&=x_1^2+(-x_3)^2+x_2^2\\
&=x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2\\
&=\|\vec{x}\|^2
\end{aligned}
\]
Geometrically, this matrix represents a rotation of \(90^\circ\) around the \(x_1\)-axis. Pick \(R\) in Figure 4: the ball looks unchanged, but the arrows show that it has turned.
We can also calculate its determinant:2
2 Determinants, rotations, and scaling. At first I thought that every matrix with determinant 1 represents a rotation. AI pointed out that this is not true. The determinant describes how oriented area or volume is scaled, not how vector length is scaled. The condition for preserving the lengths of all vectors is \[
A^TA=I
\] and a matrix satisfying it is called an orthogonal matrix. AI also told me that breaking a matrix into rotations, reflections, and scaling along different directions is related to singular value decomposition (SVD), \(A=U\Sigma V^T\). I haven’t studied any of these yet, so I’ll leave them here and explore them later.
Update (2026-10-29): Chapter 4 explained the first part. The squared length of \(A\vec{x}\) is \((A\vec{x})^T(A\vec{x})=\vec{x}^TA^TA\vec{x}\), which equals \(\vec{x}^T\vec{x}\), the squared length of \(\vec{x}\), for every \(\vec{x}\) exactly when \(A^TA=I\). A determinant of 1 says nothing like this: the shear \(\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\) keeps every area but stretches \((0,1)\) to \((1,1)\). I still haven’t studied the SVD.\[
\det(R)=1
\]


2.2 A Thought About Neural Networks and Computation
Understanding matrices as linear transformations also reminds me of neural networks.
If we temporarily ignore the nonlinear components, many computations in neural networks can be understood as a sequence of linear transformations applied to input data using a large number of parameters.
Of course, actual neural networks are much more complicated. We are ignoring bias terms, activation functions, and many other structures for now.
But from this highly simplified perspective, we can imagine an input passing through a series of matrix operations, producing new representations and eventually an output.
There is a catch in this simplification, though. Applying several matrices one after another is itself just one matrix: \(W_3(W_2(W_1\vec{x}))=(W_3W_2W_1)\vec{x}\).3 Without the nonlinear parts, a hundred layers could do nothing that a single layer couldn’t, and they could still only turn a ball into an ellipsoid. The nonlinear activation functions between the layers are what let a network bend space into more complicated shapes, which is the same question as turning a ball into a cube in note 1.4
3 Is the transformation unique? Walking downstairs one day, I had this thought. Suppose a linear transformation takes \(\vec{a}\) to \(\vec{b}\). It might be one matrix \(A\), or several, \(B\), \(C\) and \(D\), and then \(BCD=A\). My first idea was that if \(A\) is invertible, this transformation must be unique, and if \(A\) is not invertible, it might not be. AI pointed out that I was mixing up two questions. A single pair \(\vec{a}\), \(\vec{b}\) never determines a matrix: \(A\) has \(n^2\) unknowns, but \(A\vec{a}=\vec{b}\) gives only \(n\) equations. To determine \(A\), we need many pairs. If the inputs are the columns of \(X\) and the outputs are the columns of \(Y\), then \(AX=Y\) has a unique solution exactly when \(X\) has rank \(n\). So it is the data that must be invertible, not \(A\). And even when \(A\) is unique, its factors are not, because \(BCD=(BM)(M^{-1}C)D\) for any invertible \(M\).4 Training as a search for a transformation. I then thought that a neural network does the same thing with linear and nonlinear transformations, so training is the search for such a transformation. I assumed that a fully connected network is only linear however many parameters it has, that later networks added some nonlinearity with modest results, and that the Transformer succeeded because its nonlinearity let it fit the data much better. AI pointed out that a fully connected network with activation functions is already nonlinear. A result called the universal approximation theorem says that such a network, made wide enough, can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region. It also told me that fitting the training data is the wrong measure, because a lookup table fits it perfectly. What matters is generalization, how well the network does on inputs it has never seen. And it told me that the Transformer mainly changed two things. Its attention computes its mixing matrix from the input itself, and it can be trained in parallel over long sequences, which made huge scale practical. AI added that this is the common explanation, not a proven one: why these models generalize so well is still not well understood, and some other architectures come fairly close at a similar scale.
So the problem, as I understand it now, is this: given a huge set of pairs \((\vec{a}_i,\vec{b}_i)\), choose a family of functions and search it for an \(f\) whose outputs \(f(\vec{a}_i)\) come close to the \(\vec{b}_i\), in a way that carries over to new inputs. I haven’t studied any of this yet, so I’ll leave it here.This also makes me think about why GPUs are particularly suitable for these computations.
Matrix multiplication contains a large number of multiply-and-add operations that can be executed in parallel, and GPUs are designed to perform large-scale parallel computation efficiently.5
5 An idea about physical matrix multipliers. I also had an interesting thought: if some physical laws naturally perform addition or linear superposition, could we build a physical device that performs matrix multiplication directly, instead of relying entirely on conventional digital logic circuits? For example, could we use electrical currents, voltages, light, or certain physical properties of materials to perform computations through physical processes?
I later learned that related approaches already exist, such as analog computing, optical computing, and memristor crossbar architectures. In a memristor crossbar the idea is quite literal: each crossing point stores a conductance \(G\), Ohm’s law \(I=GV\) does the multiplication, and Kirchhoff’s current law adds up the currents flowing into each wire.
However, even if some physical operations can be performed with massive parallelism, it does not automatically mean that arbitrary-sized matrix multiplication can achieve \(O(1)\) complexity. Hardware scale, input/output costs, numerical precision, and data movement still matter.
This idea is somewhat outside the main topic of this post, so I may explore it separately in the future.

title: Matrices as Transformations
section: 3 From Forward Transformation to the Inverse Problem
text:
3 From Forward Transformation to the Inverse Problem
Now let’s return to our original equation:
\[
A\vec{x}=\vec{b}
\]
So far, we have assumed that \(\vec{x}\) is known, and our task is to calculate \(\vec{b}\).
We have already discussed two perspectives.
The first is to consider three known vectors \(\vec{u}\), \(\vec{v}\), and \(\vec{w}\), together with three known coefficients \(x_1\), \(x_2\), and \(x_3\), and calculate their linear combination.
The second is to consider a known input vector \(\vec{x}\) and apply a linear transformation represented by the matrix \(A\) to obtain the output vector \(\vec{b}\).
Although these perspectives are different, they produce exactly the same result.
Now, let’s reverse the question.
Suppose the matrix \(A\) is known, and the output vector \(\vec{b}\) is also known. Can we recover the original input vector \(\vec{x}\)?
From the perspective of linear combinations, we are asking:
How should we combine \(\vec{u}\), \(\vec{v}\), and \(\vec{w}\) to produce a specific vector \(\vec{b}\)?
From the perspective of linear transformations, we are asking:
If we know the transformation and its output, can we recover the original input?
For an invertible matrix, we can write:
\[
\vec{x}=A^{-1}\vec{b}
\]
But what exactly is \(A^{-1}\)?
Let’s return to our previous example:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
-1&1&0\\
0&-1&1
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}b_1\\b_2\\b_3\end{bmatrix}
\]
We can expand this into a system of equations:
\[
\begin{cases}
x_1=b_1\\
x_2-x_1=b_2\\
x_3-x_2=b_3
\end{cases}
\]
Then solve for the original variables:
\[
\begin{cases}
x_1=b_1\\
x_2=b_1+b_2\\
x_3=b_1+b_2+b_3
\end{cases}
\]
We can rewrite these equations in matrix form:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\end{bmatrix}
=
\underbrace{
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
1&1&0\\
1&1&1
\end{bmatrix}}_{A^{-1}}
\begin{bmatrix}b_1\\b_2\\b_3\end{bmatrix}
\]
So the inverse matrix is:6
6 Look at what the two matrices do. \(A\) takes differences of neighbouring entries, and \(A^{-1}\) takes running sums: \(x_3=b_1+b_2+b_3\). Summing undoes differencing, the same way integration undoes differentiation, and this pair is a small discrete version of that.\[
A^{-1}=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
1&1&0\\
1&1&1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
This means that for any given output vector \(\vec{b}\), we can find exactly one corresponding input vector \(\vec{x}\).
Therefore, the matrix \(A\) is invertible.
But does every matrix have this property?

title: Matrices as Transformations
text:
4 Linear Dependence and Independence
Let’s modify our original matrix slightly.
We keep \(\vec{u}\) and \(\vec{v}\) unchanged, but replace the third vector with:
\[
\vec{w}^*=
\begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}
\]
Now we have a new matrix:
\[
C=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&-1\\
-1&1&0\\
0&-1&1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The transformation becomes:
\[
C\vec{x}=
\begin{bmatrix}
x_1-x_3\\
x_2-x_1\\
x_3-x_2
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}b_1\\b_2\\b_3\end{bmatrix}
\]
Let’s try to solve this equation:
\[
\begin{cases}
x_1-x_3=b_1\\
x_2-x_1=b_2\\
x_3-x_2=b_3
\end{cases}
\]
If we add all three equations together, something interesting happens.
Every \(x\) term cancels out:
\[
0=b_1+b_2+b_3
\]
Therefore:
\[
b_1+b_2+b_3=0
\]
What does this mean?
First, no matter what input vector \(\vec{x}\) we choose, the output of the transformation must satisfy this condition.
Geometrically, all vectors satisfying this equation lie on a plane in three-dimensional space:
\[
b_1+b_2+b_3=0
\]
In other words, although the original input vectors can fill the entire three-dimensional space, their outputs after applying \(C\) are restricted to a two-dimensional plane (Figure 5).













Figure 5: \(C\) squeezes space onto a plane. The 27 input vectors form a grid that fills a cube in space. Press Play to transform them by \(C\): every output lands on the plane \(b_1+b_2+b_3=0\), which appears as they arrive; the edge-on view makes this obvious, because the plane and all the points collapse into one line. Switch to \(A\) to compare: its outputs fill space, and no plane holds them all.



We have lost one dimension.

4.1 What Happens to the Missing Dimension?
Let’s consider a special case:
\[
\vec{b}=
\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}
\]
The equations become:
\[
\begin{cases}
x_1-x_3=0\\
x_2-x_1=0\\
x_3-x_2=0
\end{cases}
\]
Therefore:
\[
x_1=x_2=x_3=c
\]
where \(c\) can be any real number.
This means that every vector of the form:
\[
\vec{x}=
c\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{bmatrix}
\]
will be transformed into the zero vector:
\[
C\begin{bmatrix}c\\c\\c\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}
\]
From a geometric perspective, all these vectors lie on a line passing through the origin, in the direction of \((1,1,1)\).
The entire line is collapsed into a single point: the origin.
Does this mean that all information along this direction has been erased?
Actually, there is something even more interesting.
For any input vector \(\vec{x}\), suppose we add an arbitrary amount in the direction \((1,1,1)\):
\[
\vec{x}'=
\vec{x}
+c\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{bmatrix}
\]
Then:
\[
C\vec{x}'=C\vec{x}
\]
Even though the two input vectors are different, they produce exactly the same output.
The matrix \(C\) can no longer distinguish between these inputs. In Figure 5, this is why 27 different inputs give only 19 different outputs.
This gives us a geometric interpretation of information loss: different inputs are mapped to the same output, so the original input can no longer be uniquely recovered.
In this example, the three-dimensional input space is mapped onto a two-dimensional output plane.
Interestingly, the direction that gets erased is perpendicular to the output plane (Figure 6).7
7 The lost direction and the output plane. I first assumed that the erased direction is always perpendicular to the output plane. AI pointed out that this is not true in general: the null space and the image of a matrix are not necessarily perpendicular. Here it just happens to be the case. I don’t understand why yet, so I’ll leave it for later.
Update (2026-10-29): Chapter 4 of Strang answers this. \(C\vec{x}=\vec{0}\) means that every row of \(C\) has a zero dot product with \(\vec{x}\), so the null space is always perpendicular to the row space, the space spanned by the rows. The output plane is the column space, a different subspace. The rows of \(C\) lie on the same plane \(b_1+b_2+b_3=0\) as its columns, so here the two spaces coincide, and the erased direction is perpendicular to both. In general they differ: \(\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\) erases the direction \((1,-1)\), which is perpendicular to its rows, \((1,1)\), but not to its outputs, which all lie along \((1,0)\).

4.2 Looking at the Columns of the Matrix
Now let’s return to the matrix \(C\) itself.
Its three column vectors are:
\[
\vec{u}=
\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\\0\end{bmatrix},
\quad
\vec{v}=
\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\\-1\end{bmatrix},
\quad
\vec{w}^*=
\begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}
\]
We can immediately notice that:
\[
\vec{u}+\vec{v}+\vec{w}^*=\vec{0}
\]
Or:
\[
\vec{w}^*=-\vec{u}-\vec{v}
\]
The third vector can be expressed as a linear combination of the first two vectors.
This means that although we have three vectors, there are only two independent directions.
The first two vectors already span a two-dimensional plane, and the third vector happens to lie on the same plane (Figure 6).













Figure 6: The columns of \(C\) and \(A\). The three columns of \(C\) lie on the plane \(b_1+b_2+b_3=0\), at \(120^\circ\) to each other, and add up to \(\vec{0}\); the edge-on view shows all three on one line. The dashed line is the direction \((1,1,1)\), which \(C\) sends to \(\vec{0}\). Strictly, it is an input direction while the plane holds outputs, but both live in three-dimensional space, so we can draw them together. Switch to the columns of \(A\): \(\vec{w}\) sticks out of the plane, and the dashed line drops from its tip to the plane.



Therefore, no matter how we scale and combine these three vectors, we can only produce vectors on that plane. We cannot produce any vector outside it.
This is linear dependence.
In contrast, our original three vectors \(\vec{u}\), \(\vec{v}\), and \(\vec{w}\) were linearly independent (switch Figure 6 to \(A\)).
In that example, the third vector did not lie on the plane spanned by the first two vectors. It introduced a new independent direction.
Together, those three vectors could span the entire three-dimensional space.
But in matrix \(C\), the third vector does not provide a new independent direction.
As a result, its columns can only span a two-dimensional plane.

title: Matrices as Transformations
text:
5 Rank and Dimension
From the previous examples, we can begin to understand a very important concept: rank.
For a matrix, we can ask how many dimensions are spanned by its column vectors.
Consider our original matrix:
\[
A=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
-1&1&0\\
0&-1&1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Its three column vectors are linearly independent and span the entire three-dimensional space.
Therefore:
\[
\operatorname{rank}(A)=3
\]
Now consider the modified matrix:
\[
C=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&-1\\
-1&1&0\\
0&-1&1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
Its three column vectors are linearly dependent and span only a two-dimensional plane.
Therefore:
\[
\operatorname{rank}(C)=2
\]
From the perspective of linear transformations, rank tells us how many independent directions exist in the output space, or equivalently, the dimension of the space that the transformation can reach.
For a transformation from three-dimensional space to three-dimensional space:

Rank 3 means the outputs can fill the entire three-dimensional space.
Rank 2 means the outputs are restricted to a two-dimensional plane.
Rank 1 means the outputs lie on a line.
Rank 0 means every input is transformed into the zero vector.

So we can think of rank as the number of independent dimensions preserved in the output of a linear transformation.
Of course, this is about the dimension of the entire output space, not the number of coordinates used to represent an individual vector.8
8 Rank–nullity theorem. AI told me that what we saw with \(C\), a two-dimensional output and one input direction erased, is an instance of a general theorem: \[
\operatorname{rank}(A)+\operatorname{nullity}(A)=n
\] where \(n\) is the dimension of the input space and the nullity is the dimension of the inputs that get mapped to zero. I haven’t studied it yet.
Update (2026-10-29): I studied it in chapter 3. After elimination, each of the \(n\) columns is either a pivot column or a free column. The pivot columns count the rank, and each free column gives one independent direction of the null space, so the two add up to \(n\). I wrote about it in Vector Spaces and Least Squares.

title: Matrices as Transformations
text:
6 Rank, Linear Dependence, and Invertibility
Now we can connect several concepts that initially seemed unrelated.
For our original matrix \(A\), the three column vectors are linearly independent. Its rank is 3, and its columns span the entire three-dimensional space.
Therefore, for any given \(\vec{b}\), there is exactly one solution:
\[
\vec{x}=A^{-1}\vec{b}
\]
This means that \(A\) is invertible.
But the situation is different for matrix \(C\).
Its three column vectors are linearly dependent, and its rank is only 2.
As a result, we encounter two possible situations.
First case: No solution.
If the given output vector \(\vec{b}\) does not satisfy:
\[
b_1+b_2+b_3=0
\]
then it does not lie on the plane spanned by the three column vectors.
No matter how we choose \(x_1\), \(x_2\), and \(x_3\), their linear combination cannot produce this vector.
Therefore, the equation has no solution.
Second case: Infinitely many solutions.
If the given output vector \(\vec{b}\) lies on that plane, then we can find a corresponding input.
However, because the three column vectors are linearly dependent, the third vector can be expressed as a combination of the first two.
This means that the same output can be produced by infinitely many different combinations of coefficients.
For example, for any \(\vec{b}\) satisfying \(b_1+b_2+b_3=0\), we can choose:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1&=t\\
x_2&=t+b_2\\
x_3&=t-b_1
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(t\) can be any real number.
By changing \(t\), we obtain infinitely many different input vectors \(\vec{x}\) that produce exactly the same output \(\vec{b}\).
These solutions have a familiar shape. Written as vectors,
\[
\vec{x}=
\begin{bmatrix}0\\b_2\\-b_1\end{bmatrix}
+t\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{bmatrix},
\]
they are one particular solution plus any point on the line that \(C\) sends to zero, the same line we found earlier. All the solutions differ from each other only along the erased direction. Figure 7 shows both cases in one picture.













Figure 7: Many inputs, one output. Five inputs on the line \((0,0,-1)+t(1,1,1)\), marked by hollow circles. Press Play: \(C\) sends all of them to \(\vec{b}=(1,0,-1)\), and no input at all reaches \(\vec{b}'=(0,1,1)\); the dashed line drops from \(\vec{b}'\) to the plane to show that it is off the plane. Switch to \(A\): the same five inputs go to five different outputs.



This explains why matrix \(C\) is not invertible.
One dimension of information has been lost. Even if we know the output, we cannot uniquely determine the original input.
From this perspective, linear dependence, rank, and invertibility are closely related. They describe different aspects of the same underlying problem.
Linear dependence tells us whether the column vectors of a matrix contain redundant directions.
Rank tells us how many dimensions those column vectors can span.
Invertibility tells us whether we can uniquely recover the original input from the output of a transformation.
For a \(3\times3\) matrix, if its three column vectors are linearly independent, then its rank is 3, and the matrix is invertible.
If the three column vectors are linearly dependent, then its rank is less than 3, and the matrix is not invertible.
We can also use the determinant to determine whether a square matrix is invertible:
\[
\det(A)\neq0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
A\text{ is invertible}
\]
If:
\[
\det(A)=0
\]
then the matrix does not have an ordinary inverse.
For our two examples, \(\det(A)=1\) (for a triangular matrix, the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries), and \(\det(C)=0\).
In fact, for an invertible square matrix, we have:
\[
A^{-1}=\frac{\operatorname{adj}(A)}{\det(A)}
\]
where \(\operatorname{adj}(A)\) is the adjugate matrix.
If the determinant is zero, the denominator of this formula becomes zero, so the inverse cannot be obtained from this expression.
But the deeper geometric reason for non-invertibility is what we discussed earlier: the transformation maps different inputs to the same output, making it impossible to uniquely recover the original input.
The determinant fits this picture too. As note 2 says, the determinant is the factor by which a transformation scales volume. \(C\) flattens all of three-dimensional space onto a plane, and anything flat has zero volume, so \(\det(C)\) has to be zero. A zero determinant is not a separate rule. It is the same collapse, measured as volume. You can watch this happen in Figure 3: as the two columns line up, the shaded parallelogram gets thinner and its area goes to zero.
This is something I have gradually realized while revisiting linear algebra.
Many concepts that initially appeared unrelated, such as matrices, linear combinations, linear dependence, rank, determinants, and inverse matrices, can actually be understood through the same geometric perspective of linear transformations.
When we stop focusing only on how to calculate formulas and instead try to understand what happens to vectors and entire spaces during a transformation, the connections between these concepts become much clearer.

title: Solving Linear Equations
text: In the previous post, I looked at matrices through vectors and linear transformations. This time I look at them from another angle: systems of linear equations. What interested me most was the geometry behind solving these systems, and how Gaussian elimination leads naturally to the LU decomposition.

title: Solving Linear Equations
text:
1 Lines, Planes and Their Normals
Consider two equations in two unknowns:
\[
\begin{cases}
x-2y=1,\\
3x+2y=11.
\end{cases}
\]
Each equation describes a line in the plane, and the solution is the point where the two lines cross, \((x,y)=(3,1)\) (Figure 1). In matrix form, the system is
\[
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\3&2\end{bmatrix}}_{A}
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}}_{\vec{x}}
=
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1\\11\end{bmatrix}}_{\vec{b}}
\]






  
  
  
  
  
  
  n1
  n2


  One point
  No solution
  Infinitely many







Figure 1: Two equations, two lines. Each equation is a line, and the solution is where they cross. The arrows are the normal vectors \(\vec{n}_1=(1,-2)\) and \(\vec{n}_2=(3,2)\), drawn at a third of their length. The buttons replace the second line with one whose normal is \(2\vec{n}_1\): a parallel line with no solution, or the same line with infinitely many.



With three equations in three unknowns, each equation describes a plane in space, and the solution is the point the three planes share. For example,
\[
\begin{cases}
x+y+z=4,\\
x-y+z=2,\\
2x-z=0
\end{cases}
\]
has the solution \((x,y,z)=(1,1,2)\) (Figure 2). The geometry changes from lines to planes, but the algebra is still \(A\vec{x}=\vec{b}\).













Figure 2: Three equations, three planes. Each pair of planes meets in a line (dark), and the three lines pass through the solution \((1,1,2)\). The buttons replace the third plane with one whose normal is the sum of the other two, \(\vec{n}_3=\vec{n}_1+\vec{n}_2\): depending on its right-hand side, the planes have no common point or a whole common line. Drag the figure to look from another side.



Whether the lines or planes meet in a single point depends on how they are tilted, and a plane’s tilt is described by its normal vector, which I remember from high-school geometry. The plane \(ax+by+cz=d\) has the normal vector \(\vec{n}=(a,b,c)\), assuming \((a,b,c)\ne(0,0,0)\). To see why, take any two points \(P_1=(x_1,y_1,z_1)\) and \(P_2=(x_2,y_2,z_2)\) on the plane. Both satisfy its equation, and subtracting the two equations gives, in the language of the dot product,
\[
(a,b,c)\cdot(x_1-x_2,\ y_1-y_2,\ z_1-z_2)=0
\]
The second vector runs along the plane. Since this holds for any two points, \((a,b,c)\) is perpendicular to every direction in the plane, which is exactly what a normal vector is. In the same way, the line \(ax+by=c\) has the normal \((a,b)\).
The normals tell us when a unique solution exists. In two dimensions, independent normals give two lines that are not parallel, so they cross at one point. Dependent normals give parallel or coincident lines, so there is either no solution or infinitely many. In three dimensions, three independent normals mean the planes meet at exactly one point. If the normals span fewer than three directions, a unique solution is impossible, and the system has no solution or infinitely many, depending on whether the equations are consistent. In matrix language, the number of independent normal vectors is the rank of \(A\).

title: Solving Linear Equations
text:
2 What Elimination Does Geometrically
To solve a system, we usually eliminate variables until it becomes upper triangular. I found it more interesting to ask what each step means geometrically.
Go back to the two lines and replace the second equation with the second equation minus three times the first:
\[
(3x+2y)-3(x-2y)=11-3
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
8y=8
\]
The new line, \(y=1\), is different from the original second line, but it still passes through \((3,1)\). The solution is unchanged because the step can be undone: adding three times the first equation back gives the original second equation.
The normal vectors change in the same way as the equations:
\[
\vec{n}_2'=\vec{n}_2-3\vec{n}_1=(3,2)-3(1,-2)=(0,8)
\]
So subtracting a multiple of one equation from another turns the second line around the fixed intersection point (Figure 3). Elimination picks the multiple that makes \(\vec{n}_2'\) point straight up: the line becomes horizontal, \(x\) disappears from its equation, and we can read off \(y=1\).






  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  n1
  n2


  multiplier ℓ  0.00
  Original
  Eliminate x







Figure 3: Elimination turns a line around the solution. The second equation is replaced by itself minus \(\ell\) times the first. The second line turns around \((3,1)\), and its normal vector changes from \(\vec{n}_2\) to \(\vec{n}_2-\ell\vec{n}_1\); the dotted segment is the step \(-\ell\vec{n}_1\), with the normals again at a third of their length. Move the slider, or press “Eliminate x” to go to \(\ell=3\), where the line becomes \(y=1\).



The same idea applies in three dimensions. Replacing one plane’s equation by a combination of two equations changes that plane, but keeps the line where the two planes meet. Elimination keeps turning planes like this (Figure 4) until the system is upper triangular: the last plane is horizontal, the one above it has no \(x\) in its equation, and we can read off \(z\), then \(y\), then \(x\).














Figure 4: Elimination in three dimensions. Elimination on the three planes of Figure 2, one step at a time. Each step subtracts a multiple of one equation from another, so the changing plane turns around the line it shares with the other plane (bold), and all three planes keep passing through \((1,1,2)\). After step 3, the system is upper triangular: \(x+y+z=4\), \(-2y=-2\) and \(-3z=-6\). Drag the figure to look from another side.

title: Solving Linear Equations
text:
3 Recording Elimination: \(PA=LU\)
Gaussian elimination turns \(A\) into an upper triangular matrix \(U\). Instead of treating it as a temporary calculation, we can record the operations that produced \(U\). In the two-line example, subtracting three times the first row from the second is itself a matrix:
\[
E=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\-3&1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
EA=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\0&8\end{bmatrix}=U
\]
Undoing the step gives \(A=E^{-1}U\):
\[
A=
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\3&1\end{bmatrix}}_{L}
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\0&8\end{bmatrix}}_{U}
\]
That is an LU decomposition. \(U\) is what elimination produces, and the lower triangular \(L\) stores the multiplier, \(3\), in a form that rebuilds \(A\).
With more than one step, we need one fact about inverses. For a square matrix \(A\), the inverse \(A^{-1}\), when it exists, satisfies \(A^{-1}A=AA^{-1}=I\), and the inverse of a product reverses the order:
\[
(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}
\]
This makes sense if we think of matrices as transformations applied one after another: \(AB\) applies \(B\) first and then \(A\), so to undo it, we first undo \(A\), then undo \(B\).
The three planes above take three steps: subtract \(1\) times row 1 from row 2 (\(E_{21}\)), \(2\) times row 1 from row 3 (\(E_{31}\)), and then \(1\) times the new row 2 from row 3 (\(E_{32}\)):
\[
E_{32}E_{31}E_{21}A=U=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&1\\0&-2&0\\0&0&-3\end{bmatrix}
\]
Undoing the three steps in reverse order,
\[
A=E_{21}^{-1}E_{31}^{-1}E_{32}^{-1}U=
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\1&1&0\\2&1&1\end{bmatrix}}_{L}U
\]
\(L\) holds the three multipliers, \(1\), \(2\) and \(1\), each in the position of the entry it eliminated. The reversed order is what keeps them clean. The forward product \(E_{32}E_{31}E_{21}\) has \(-1\) in its bottom-left corner, not \(-2\): it changes row 3 using row 2 after row 2 has already been changed, so the multipliers mix. Multiplied in the reverse order, the inverses simply put each multiplier in its place.
Why keep \(L\)? Suppose we need to solve \(A\vec{x}=\vec{b}\) for many right-hand sides \(\vec{b}\) while \(A\) stays the same. With \(A=LU\), each new \(\vec{b}\) needs only two triangular systems,
\[
L\vec{y}=\vec{b},\qquad U\vec{x}=\vec{y}
\]
solved by forward and back substitution. We could also save the row operations and replay them on each new \(\vec{b}\). LU is a structured way to do exactly that. The saving is large: eliminating an \(n\times n\) matrix takes about \(n^3/3\) multiplications, while the two triangular solves take about \(n^2\).
One complication remains: not every invertible matrix can be factored this way without row exchanges. For example,
\[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}
\]
is invertible, but its first pivot is zero, so the rows must be exchanged first. A permutation matrix \(P\) records the exchanges, which gives the general form
\[
PA=LU
\]
To solve \(A\vec{x}=\vec{b}\) with it, we permute the right-hand side the same way: \(LU\vec{x}=P\vec{b}\).
For me, the main idea is that LU is not a separate trick from Gaussian elimination. It is the work elimination already does, written down so that it can be reused.

title: Solving Linear Equations
text:
4 Transpose, for Now
The transpose \(A^T\) exchanges the rows and columns of \(A\); I picture its entries flipped across the main diagonal. A matrix with \(A=A^T\) is called symmetric. Like the inverse, the transpose of a product reverses the order, \((AB)^T=B^TA^T\). I can verify this from the definitions, but the connection between the transpose, dot products and orthogonality will be more interesting later, so I’ll leave it here.1
1 Update (2026-10-29): The connection showed up in the next post. A dot product can be written with the transpose, \(\vec{x}\cdot\vec{y}=\vec{x}^T\vec{y}\), so \(A^T\vec{e}\) collects the dot products of \(\vec{e}\) with every column of \(A\) at once. Least squares needs the error to be perpendicular to every column, \(A^T(\vec{y}-A\hat{\vec{w}})=\vec{0}\), and that gives the normal equations. See Vector Spaces and Least Squares.For now, the two ideas I want to keep from this post are the geometric meaning of elimination and the way LU records it.

title: 把矩阵看作变换
text: 本文译自英文原文 Matrices as Transformations，如有出入，以英文版为准。

title: 把矩阵看作变换
text:
1 从向量的组合到矩阵
前面我们讨论了向量的一些基本概念和运算。现在，我们从三个向量开始：
\[
\vec{u}=
\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\\0\end{bmatrix},
\quad
\vec{v}=
\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\\-1\end{bmatrix},
\quad
\vec{w}=
\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}
\]
假设我们分别用 \(x_1\)、\(x_2\)、\(x_3\) 去缩放这三个向量，再把它们加起来：
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1\vec{u}+x_2\vec{v}+x_3\vec{w}
&=
x_1\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\\0\end{bmatrix}
+x_2\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\\-1\end{bmatrix}
+x_3\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}\\
&=
\begin{bmatrix}
x_1\\
x_2-x_1\\
x_3-x_2
\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
\]
这很好理解。我们有三个向量，可以用不同的数去乘它们，把它们拉长、缩短，甚至反向。最后把它们加起来，得到一个新的向量（图 1）。













图 1: 用三个向量组合出 \(\vec{b}\)。 缩放后的向量 \(x_1\vec{u}\)、\(x_2\vec{v}\)、\(x_3\vec{w}\) 都从原点出发，浅色虚线是 \(\vec{u}\)、\(\vec{v}\)、\(\vec{w}\) 本身。点线补出平行四边形：先得到 \(x_1\vec{u}+x_2\vec{v}\)，再加上 \(x_3\vec{w}\) 就得到 \(\vec{b}\)，它的坐标标在旁边。移动滑块可以改变 \(x_1\)、\(x_2\)、\(x_3\)，拖动图形可以换个角度看。



但我们可以把这个式子写得更简洁：
\[
\underbrace{
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
-1&1&0\\
0&-1&1
\end{bmatrix}}_A
\underbrace{
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\end{bmatrix}}_{\vec{x}}
=
\underbrace{
\begin{bmatrix}
x_1\\
x_2-x_1\\
x_3-x_2
\end{bmatrix}}_{\vec{b}}
\]
或者干脆写成：
\[
A\vec{x}=\vec{b}
\]
这个式子虽然看起来更简单，但我觉得它带来了一个非常有意思的视角转换。
之前，\(x_1\)、\(x_2\)、\(x_3\) 只是用来缩放向量的三个系数。现在，我们把这三个数合成了一个新的向量 \(\vec{x}\)。
从这个角度看，矩阵 \(A\) 对输入向量 \(\vec{x}\) 做了一次线性变换。之所以叫“线性”，是因为它和向量的两种基本运算相容：\(A(\vec{x}+\vec{y})=A\vec{x}+A\vec{y}\)，\(A(c\vec{x})=cA\vec{x}\)。先对输入做加法或数乘再变换，和先变换再做加法或数乘，结果一样。
我们可以直接观察这个变换：
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1&\longrightarrow x_1\\
x_2&\longrightarrow x_2-x_1\\
x_3&\longrightarrow x_3-x_2
\end{aligned}
\]
也就是说，原来的向量 \((x_1,x_2,x_3)\) 被变换成了另一个向量。图 2 展示了整个空间同时被变换的过程。













图 2: 把矩阵看作变换。 点击“播放”，观察 \(A\) 如何变换空间。\(\vec{e}_1\)、\(\vec{e}_2\)、\(\vec{e}_3\) 是沿坐标轴的单位向量，单位立方体随它们一起变换：这三条棱变成了三列 \(\vec{u}\)、\(\vec{v}\)、\(\vec{w}\)。输入 \(\vec{x}=(1,0.5,1.5)\)，也就是 \(1\vec{e}_1+0.5\vec{e}_2+1.5\vec{e}_3\)，变成了 \(1\vec{u}+0.5\vec{v}+1.5\vec{w}=\vec{b}\)，和 图 1 中的向量相同。这就是两种视角一致的原因。



对于任意给定的输入 \(\vec{x}\)，我们都可以作用矩阵 \(A\)，得到对应的输出 \(\vec{b}\)。
其实，这两种视角描述的是完全相同的数学运算。
一种视角把矩阵与向量的乘法看作矩阵各列的线性组合，另一种把它看作作用在输入向量上的线性变换。
\(A\vec{x}\) 还有第三种读法，也是我们手算时通常用的方法：\(\vec{b}\) 的每一个分量，都是 \(A\) 的某一行与 \(\vec{x}\) 的点积。\(A\) 的第二行是 \((-1,1,0)\)，而 \((-1,1,0)\cdot(x_1,x_2,x_3)=x_2-x_1\)，正好是 \(\vec{b}\) 的第二个分量。所以，上一篇里的点积其实藏在每一次矩阵乘法里。
正是从这里，我开始从几何的角度理解矩阵：矩阵不只是一堆数，它还可以表示空间中的一个线性变换。

title: 把矩阵看作变换
text:
2 把矩阵看作线性变换
如果矩阵表示一个线性变换，就会自然地产生一个问题：作用这个变换之后，空间里的向量到底发生了什么？
我们不只看一个向量，而是看一整组向量。
假设输入向量 \(\vec{x}\) 可以取三维空间中的任意值。作用矩阵 \(A\) 之后，这些向量会构成一个什么样的集合？
或者把问题问得更具体一些。
假设所有输入向量都限制在三维单位球内：
\[
x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2\leq1
\]
经过一次线性变换，这个球会变成什么？
它会被拉伸成一个椭球吗？会被压到一个二维平面上，变成一个椭圆盘吗？甚至会坍缩成一条线段或一个点吗？
这些都有可能。1 图 3 在低一维的情形下展示了同样的想法：球变成了圆盘，它的像可以是一个椭圆、一条线段，或者一个点。
1 线性变换能产生什么形状？ 我一开始的想法是，线性变换几乎可以把一个球变成任意形状，比如立方体或长方体。和 AI 一起探索时，它指出这是做不到的：球在线性变换下只能变成椭球，或者椭球的某种退化形式，比如椭圆盘、线段或一个点。要把球变成立方体，需要非线性变换。为什么会有这个限制，我还没有研究过，留到以后。





  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  uv
  


  Identity
  Stretch
  Rotate
  Shear
  Project
  Dependent







图 3: 二维中的矩阵。 矩阵 \(A\) 的两列是 \(\vec{u}\) 和 \(\vec{v}\)。拖动它们的端点，或者选一个例子。网格显示整个平面被变到了哪里，单位圆变成实线的曲线，阴影部分的单位正方形变成一个平行四边形，面积为 \(|\det A|\)。当 \(\vec{u}\) 和 \(\vec{v}\) 落在同一条直线上时，整个平面就被压到这条直线上。



我觉得这个视角特别有意思。我们不再只研究一个向量怎么变化，而是研究一整组向量是怎样被变换的。
从这个角度看，矩阵可以描述各种线性变换，比如拉伸、压缩、旋转、反射和投影。
我们还可以研究在这些变换中，哪些性质被保留了下来，比如向量的长度、向量之间的夹角，以及变换后空间的维数。

2.1 线性变换的几个例子
先看一个简单的例子：单位矩阵。
\[
I=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
0&1&0\\
0&0&1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
对任意向量：
\[
I\vec{x}=\vec{x}
\]
它不改变输入向量的任何坐标。原来的向量是什么，变换之后还是什么。
再看另外两个矩阵：
\[
P_1=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
0&0&0\\
0&0&0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
P_2=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
0&1&0\\
0&0&0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
它们的变换是：
\[
P_1
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
P_2
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\0\end{bmatrix}
\]
图 4 展示了这些矩阵对单位球做了什么。













图 4: 各个矩阵对单位球的作用。 本节各个矩阵作用下的单位球和单位向量 \(\vec{e}_1\)、\(\vec{e}_2\)、\(\vec{e}_3\)。选一个矩阵观察变换过程，拖动图形可以旋转视角。



第一个矩阵只保留 \(x_1\) 坐标，去掉了另外两个坐标。
如果原来的输入集合是一个三维的球，变换后的集合会完全落在 \(x_1\) 轴上，成为一条线段。
第二个矩阵保留 \(x_1\) 和 \(x_2\)，去掉了 \(x_3\)。
同一个三维的球会变成 \(x_1x_2\) 平面上的一个圆盘。
换句话说，这些矩阵降低了原集合的维数，丢掉了一部分信息。
如果我们修改矩阵的某些元素，比如把 \(P_2\) 的一个非零对角元从 1 改成 2，得到的圆盘就会变成椭圆盘（图 4 中的第四个例子）。
如果一个矩阵保留全部三个坐标，只是按不同的比例缩放它们，又会怎样？例如：
\[
S=
\begin{bmatrix}
1.5&0&0\\
0&1&0\\
0&0&0.5
\end{bmatrix}
\]
它的变换是：
\[
S
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}1.5x_1\\x_2\\0.5x_3\end{bmatrix}
\]
在 图 4 中选 \(S\)：球沿 \(x_1\) 轴被拉长、沿 \(x_3\) 轴被压扁，变成一个椭球。和 \(P_1\)、\(P_2\) 不同，\(S\) 没有去掉任何坐标，所以结果仍然是三维的，也没有丢失信息。
再看另一个矩阵：
\[
R=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
0&0&-1\\
0&1&0
\end{bmatrix}
\]
它做的变换是：
\[
R\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\-x_3\\x_2\end{bmatrix}
\]
这个变换有一个有意思的性质。
它不改变向量的长度：
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|R\vec{x}\|^2
&=x_1^2+(-x_3)^2+x_2^2\\
&=x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2\\
&=\|\vec{x}\|^2
\end{aligned}
\]
从几何上看，这个矩阵表示绕 \(x_1\) 轴旋转 \(90^\circ\)。在 图 4 中选 \(R\)：球看起来没变，但箭头显示它已经转过去了。
我们还可以算出它的行列式：2
2 行列式、旋转与缩放。 一开始我以为，所有行列式为 1 的矩阵都表示旋转。AI 指出并不是这样。行列式描述的是有向面积或体积的缩放倍数，而不是向量长度的缩放倍数。保持所有向量长度不变的条件是 \[
A^TA=I
\] 满足这个条件的矩阵叫作正交矩阵。AI 还告诉我，把一个矩阵拆成旋转、反射以及沿不同方向的缩放，和奇异值分解（SVD） \(A=U\Sigma V^T\) 有关。这些我都还没有学过，先留在这里，以后再探索。
更新（2026-10-29）： 第四章解释了前一半。\(A\vec{x}\) 长度的平方是 \((A\vec{x})^T(A\vec{x})=\vec{x}^TA^TA\vec{x}\)，它对每个 \(\vec{x}\) 都等于 \(\vec{x}\) 长度的平方 \(\vec{x}^T\vec{x}\)，当且仅当 \(A^TA=I\)。行列式等于 1 说明不了这一点：剪切矩阵 \(\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\) 保持所有面积不变，却把 \((0,1)\) 拉长成 \((1,1)\)。SVD 我仍然没有学。\[
\det(R)=1
\]


2.2 关于神经网络和计算的一点想法
把矩阵理解为线性变换，也让我想到了神经网络。
如果暂时忽略非线性的部分，神经网络中的很多计算都可以理解为：用大量参数对输入数据依次施加一系列线性变换。
当然，真正的神经网络要复杂得多。我们暂时忽略了偏置项、激活函数和许多其他结构。
但从这个高度简化的视角，我们可以想象一个输入经过一连串矩阵运算，产生新的表示，最后得到输出。
不过，这个简化里有一个陷阱。接连作用几个矩阵，本身也只是一个矩阵：\(W_3(W_2(W_1\vec{x}))=(W_3W_2W_1)\vec{x}\)。3没有非线性的部分，一百层能做到的事，一层也能做到，而且它们仍然只能把球变成椭球。层与层之间的非线性激活函数，才让网络能把空间弯成更复杂的形状，这和注 1 里把球变成立方体的问题是同一个问题。4
3 变换是唯一的吗？ 有一天下楼的时候，我想到一个问题。假设一个线性变换把 \(\vec{a}\) 变成 \(\vec{b}\)，它可能是一个矩阵 \(A\)，也可能是几个矩阵 \(B\)、\(C\)、\(D\)，那么 \(BCD=A\)。我最初的想法是：如果 \(A\) 可逆，这个变换就一定是唯一的；如果 \(A\) 不可逆，它就不一定唯一。AI 指出我把两个问题混在了一起。单独一对 \(\vec{a}\)、\(\vec{b}\) 永远确定不了一个矩阵：\(A\) 有 \(n^2\) 个未知数，而 \(A\vec{a}=\vec{b}\) 只给出 \(n\) 个方程。要确定 \(A\)，需要很多对数据。把输入作为 \(X\) 的列、输出作为 \(Y\) 的列，那么当且仅当 \(X\) 的秩为 \(n\) 时，\(AX=Y\) 才有唯一解。所以需要可逆的是数据，而不是 \(A\)。而且即使 \(A\) 唯一，它的分解也不唯一，因为对任意可逆矩阵 \(M\)，都有 \(BCD=(BM)(M^{-1}C)D\)。4 把训练看作寻找变换。 接着我想到，神经网络做的是同样的事，只不过用的是线性加非线性的变换，所以训练就是在寻找这样一个变换。我原以为全连接网络不管参数多大都只是线性变换，后来的网络加了一些非线性但效果一般，而 Transformer 成功是因为它的非线性让拟合程度大大提高。AI 指出，带激活函数的全连接网络本身就是非线性的；有一个叫万能逼近定理的结果说，这样的网络只要足够宽，就能在有界区域上逼近任何连续函数。它还告诉我，训练数据上的拟合程度不是正确的衡量标准，因为一张查找表就能完美拟合；真正重要的是泛化能力，也就是网络在从没见过的输入上表现如何。它还告诉我，Transformer 主要改变了两点：它的注意力机制根据输入本身算出混合矩阵；它能在长序列上并行训练，这让巨大的规模成为可能。AI 也补充说，这只是常见的解释，并没有被证明：这些模型为什么泛化得这么好，目前还没有被很好地理解，而且在相近的规模下，一些其他结构的效果也相差不远。
所以按我现在的理解，问题是这样的：给定海量的数据对 \((\vec{a}_i,\vec{b}_i)\)，选定一个函数族，在其中寻找一个 \(f\)，让输出 \(f(\vec{a}_i)\) 接近 \(\vec{b}_i\)，并且这种效果能推广到新的输入上。这些我都还没有学过，先记在这里。这也让我想到，为什么 GPU 特别适合做这些计算。
矩阵乘法包含大量可以并行执行的乘加运算，而 GPU 正是为高效地进行大规模并行计算而设计的。5
5 关于物理矩阵乘法器的一个想法。 我还有一个有意思的想法：如果某些物理规律天然就在做加法或线性叠加，我们能不能造一个直接做矩阵乘法的物理装置，而不完全依赖传统的数字逻辑电路？比如，能不能利用电流、电压、光，或者材料的某些物理性质，通过物理过程来完成计算？
后来我了解到，相关的方法已经存在，比如模拟计算、光计算和忆阻器交叉阵列架构。在忆阻器交叉阵列里，这个想法几乎是字面意义上的：每个交叉点存储一个电导 \(G\)，欧姆定律 \(I=GV\) 完成乘法，基尔霍夫电流定律把流进每根导线的电流加起来。
不过，即使某些物理操作可以大规模并行地完成，也不意味着任意规模的矩阵乘法都能达到 \(O(1)\) 复杂度。硬件规模、输入输出的开销、数值精度和数据搬运仍然很重要。
这个想法有点偏离本文的主题，所以以后可能单独探索。

title: 把矩阵看作变换
text:
3 从正向变换到逆问题
现在回到最初的方程：
\[
A\vec{x}=\vec{b}
\]
到目前为止，我们都假设 \(\vec{x}\) 已知，任务是算出 \(\vec{b}\)。
我们已经讨论了两种视角。
第一种是：已知三个向量 \(\vec{u}\)、\(\vec{v}\)、\(\vec{w}\) 和三个系数 \(x_1\)、\(x_2\)、\(x_3\)，计算它们的线性组合。
第二种是：已知输入向量 \(\vec{x}\)，对它施加矩阵 \(A\) 所表示的线性变换，得到输出向量 \(\vec{b}\)。
这两种视角虽然不同，得到的结果却完全一样。
现在，我们把问题反过来。
假设矩阵 \(A\) 已知，输出向量 \(\vec{b}\) 也已知。我们能还原出原来的输入向量 \(\vec{x}\) 吗？
从线性组合的角度，我们问的是：
应该怎样组合 \(\vec{u}\)、\(\vec{v}\)、\(\vec{w}\)，才能得到一个指定的向量 \(\vec{b}\)？
从线性变换的角度，我们问的是：
如果知道变换和它的输出，能不能还原出原来的输入？
对于可逆矩阵，我们可以写成：
\[
\vec{x}=A^{-1}\vec{b}
\]
但 \(A^{-1}\) 到底是什么？
回到前面的例子：
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
-1&1&0\\
0&-1&1
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}b_1\\b_2\\b_3\end{bmatrix}
\]
可以把它展开成一个方程组：
\[
\begin{cases}
x_1=b_1\\
x_2-x_1=b_2\\
x_3-x_2=b_3
\end{cases}
\]
然后解出原来的变量：
\[
\begin{cases}
x_1=b_1\\
x_2=b_1+b_2\\
x_3=b_1+b_2+b_3
\end{cases}
\]
再把这些方程写成矩阵形式：
\[
\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\end{bmatrix}
=
\underbrace{
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
1&1&0\\
1&1&1
\end{bmatrix}}_{A^{-1}}
\begin{bmatrix}b_1\\b_2\\b_3\end{bmatrix}
\]
所以逆矩阵是：6
6 看看这两个矩阵各自做了什么。\(A\) 求相邻分量的差，\(A^{-1}\) 求累加和：\(x_3=b_1+b_2+b_3\)。求和抵消了求差，就像积分抵消了求导，这一对矩阵就是它的一个小小的离散版本。\[
A^{-1}=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
1&1&0\\
1&1&1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
这意味着，对于任意给定的输出向量 \(\vec{b}\)，我们都能找到唯一一个对应的输入向量 \(\vec{x}\)。
所以，矩阵 \(A\) 是可逆的。
但是，是不是每个矩阵都有这个性质？

title: 把矩阵看作变换
text:
4 线性相关与线性无关
我们把原来的矩阵稍微改一下。
保持 \(\vec{u}\) 和 \(\vec{v}\) 不变，把第三个向量换成：
\[
\vec{w}^*=
\begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}
\]
现在得到一个新的矩阵：
\[
C=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&-1\\
-1&1&0\\
0&-1&1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
变换变成了：
\[
C\vec{x}=
\begin{bmatrix}
x_1-x_3\\
x_2-x_1\\
x_3-x_2
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}b_1\\b_2\\b_3\end{bmatrix}
\]
我们试着解这个方程：
\[
\begin{cases}
x_1-x_3=b_1\\
x_2-x_1=b_2\\
x_3-x_2=b_3
\end{cases}
\]
如果把三个方程加起来，有意思的事情发生了。
所有 \(x\) 项都抵消了：
\[
0=b_1+b_2+b_3
\]
因此：
\[
b_1+b_2+b_3=0
\]
这意味着什么？
首先，无论选择什么输入向量 \(\vec{x}\)，变换的输出都必须满足这个条件。
从几何上看，满足这个方程的所有向量都落在三维空间中的一个平面上：
\[
b_1+b_2+b_3=0
\]
换句话说，虽然原来的输入向量可以充满整个三维空间，但作用 \(C\) 之后，它们的输出被限制在一个二维平面上（图 5）。













图 5: \(C\) 把空间压到一个平面上。 27 个输入向量组成的网格占满了空间中的一个立方体。点击“播放”，用 \(C\) 变换它们：所有输出都落在平面 \(b_1+b_2+b_3=0\) 上，这个平面随着点的到达逐渐显现；切换到侧面视角会看得更清楚，平面和所有的点都缩成了一条线。切换到 \(A\) 作对比：它的输出充满整个空间，没有哪个平面能装下它们。



我们丢掉了一个维度。

4.1 丢掉的那个维度去哪了？
考虑一个特殊情况：
\[
\vec{b}=
\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}
\]
方程变成：
\[
\begin{cases}
x_1-x_3=0\\
x_2-x_1=0\\
x_3-x_2=0
\end{cases}
\]
因此：
\[
x_1=x_2=x_3=c
\]
其中 \(c\) 可以是任意实数。
这意味着，所有形如
\[
\vec{x}=
c\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{bmatrix}
\]
的向量，都会被变换成零向量：
\[
C\begin{bmatrix}c\\c\\c\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}
\]
从几何上看，这些向量都落在一条经过原点、方向为 \((1,1,1)\) 的直线上。
整条直线被压缩成了一个点：原点。
这是不是意味着，沿这个方向的所有信息都被抹掉了？
其实，还有更有意思的事情。
对任意输入向量 \(\vec{x}\)，假设我们沿 \((1,1,1)\) 方向加上任意的量：
\[
\vec{x}'=
\vec{x}
+c\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{bmatrix}
\]
那么：
\[
C\vec{x}'=C\vec{x}
\]
即使两个输入向量不同，它们的输出也完全一样。
矩阵 \(C\) 已经无法区分这些输入了。这也是为什么在 图 5 中，27 个不同的输入只得到 19 个不同的输出。
这给了信息丢失一个几何上的解释：不同的输入被映射到同一个输出，所以原来的输入再也无法被唯一地还原。
在这个例子里，三维的输入空间被映射到了一个二维的输出平面上。
有意思的是，被抹掉的方向正好垂直于输出平面（图 6）。7
7 丢掉的方向与输出平面。 我原以为被抹掉的方向总是垂直于输出平面。AI 指出一般并非如此：矩阵的零空间和像空间不一定互相垂直，这里只是恰好如此。我还不明白其中的原因，留到以后。
更新（2026-10-29）： Strang 的第四章回答了这个问题。\(C\vec{x}=\vec{0}\) 意味着 \(C\) 的每一行与 \(\vec{x}\) 的点积都是零，所以零空间总是垂直于行空间，也就是由各行张成的空间。输出平面是列空间，是另一个子空间。\(C\) 的各行和各列落在同一个平面 \(b_1+b_2+b_3=0\) 上，所以这里两个空间恰好重合，被抹掉的方向同时垂直于两者。一般情况下二者不同：\(\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\) 抹掉的方向是 \((1,-1)\)，它垂直于矩阵的行 \((1,1)\)，却不垂直于输出，因为输出全都在 \((1,0)\) 方向上。

4.2 看看矩阵的列
现在回到矩阵 \(C\) 本身。
它的三个列向量是：
\[
\vec{u}=
\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\\0\end{bmatrix},
\quad
\vec{v}=
\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\\-1\end{bmatrix},
\quad
\vec{w}^*=
\begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}
\]
我们马上可以注意到：
\[
\vec{u}+\vec{v}+\vec{w}^*=\vec{0}
\]
或者：
\[
\vec{w}^*=-\vec{u}-\vec{v}
\]
第三个向量可以表示成前两个向量的线性组合。
这意味着，虽然我们有三个向量，但只有两个独立的方向。
前两个向量已经张成了一个二维平面，而第三个向量恰好落在同一个平面上（图 6）。













图 6: \(C\) 和 \(A\) 的列。 \(C\) 的三列都落在平面 \(b_1+b_2+b_3=0\) 上，两两之间夹角为 \(120^\circ\)，加起来等于 \(\vec{0}\)；在侧面视角下，三者都在一条线上。虚线是方向 \((1,1,1)\)，\(C\) 把它变成 \(\vec{0}\)。严格地说，它是一个输入方向，而平面上放的是输出，但两者都在三维空间里，所以可以画在一起。切换到 \(A\) 的列：\(\vec{w}\) 伸出了平面，虚线从它的端点垂直落到平面上。



因此，无论怎样缩放和组合这三个向量，我们都只能得到这个平面上的向量，得不到平面外的任何向量。
这就是线性相关。
相比之下，最初的三个向量 \(\vec{u}\)、\(\vec{v}\)、\(\vec{w}\) 是线性无关的（把 图 6 切换到 \(A\)）。
在那个例子里，第三个向量不在前两个向量张成的平面上，它引入了一个新的独立方向。
这三个向量合在一起，可以张成整个三维空间。
但在矩阵 \(C\) 中，第三个向量没有提供新的独立方向。
结果，它的各列只能张成一个二维平面。

title: 把矩阵看作变换
text:
5 秩与维数
从前面的例子，我们可以开始理解一个非常重要的概念：秩。
对于一个矩阵，我们可以问：它的列向量张成了多少维？
考虑最初的矩阵：
\[
A=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\
-1&1&0\\
0&-1&1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
它的三个列向量线性无关，张成了整个三维空间。
因此：
\[
\operatorname{rank}(A)=3
\]
再考虑修改后的矩阵：
\[
C=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&-1\\
-1&1&0\\
0&-1&1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
它的三个列向量线性相关，只张成了一个二维平面。
因此：
\[
\operatorname{rank}(C)=2
\]
从线性变换的角度看，秩告诉我们输出空间里有多少个独立方向，也就是变换所能到达的空间的维数。
对于从三维空间到三维空间的变换：

秩为 3，意味着输出可以充满整个三维空间。
秩为 2，意味着输出被限制在一个二维平面上。
秩为 1，意味着输出落在一条直线上。
秩为 0，意味着每个输入都被变换成零向量。

所以，我们可以把秩看作线性变换的输出中保留下来的独立维数。
当然，这里说的是整个输出空间的维数，而不是表示单个向量所用的坐标个数。8
8 秩–零化度定理。 AI 告诉我，我们在 \(C\) 上看到的现象，即二维的输出加上一个被抹掉的输入方向，是一个一般定理的特例： \[
\operatorname{rank}(A)+\operatorname{nullity}(A)=n
\] 其中 \(n\) 是输入空间的维数，零化度是被映射为零的那些输入所构成的子空间的维数。这个定理我还没有学。
更新（2026-10-29）： 我在第三章学了它。消元之后，\(n\) 列中的每一列要么是主元列，要么是自由列。主元列的个数就是秩，每个自由列给出零空间的一个独立方向，所以两者加起来等于 \(n\)。我在《向量空间与最小二乘》里写了这件事。

title: 把矩阵看作变换
text:
6 秩、线性相关与可逆性
现在，我们可以把几个起初看起来毫不相干的概念联系起来了。
对于最初的矩阵 \(A\)，三个列向量线性无关。它的秩是 3，各列张成了整个三维空间。
因此，对于任意给定的 \(\vec{b}\)，都有且只有一个解：
\[
\vec{x}=A^{-1}\vec{b}
\]
这意味着 \(A\) 是可逆的。
但矩阵 \(C\) 的情况不一样。
它的三个列向量线性相关，秩只有 2。
于是，我们会遇到两种可能的情况。
第一种情况：无解。
如果给定的输出向量 \(\vec{b}\) 不满足
\[
b_1+b_2+b_3=0
\]
它就不在三个列向量张成的平面上。
无论怎样选择 \(x_1\)、\(x_2\)、\(x_3\)，它们的线性组合都得不到这个向量。
因此，方程无解。
第二种情况：无穷多个解。
如果给定的输出向量 \(\vec{b}\) 落在这个平面上，我们就能找到一个对应的输入。
但是，因为三个列向量线性相关，第三个向量可以表示成前两个的组合。
这意味着，同一个输出可以由无穷多种不同的系数组合得到。
例如，对任意满足 \(b_1+b_2+b_3=0\) 的 \(\vec{b}\)，我们可以取：
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1&=t\\
x_2&=t+b_2\\
x_3&=t-b_1
\end{aligned}
\]
其中 \(t\) 可以是任意实数。
改变 \(t\)，就得到无穷多个不同的输入向量 \(\vec{x}\)，它们产生完全相同的输出 \(\vec{b}\)。
这些解有一个熟悉的形状。写成向量，
\[
\vec{x}=
\begin{bmatrix}0\\b_2\\-b_1\end{bmatrix}
+t\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{bmatrix},
\]
它们是一个特解，加上 \(C\) 映射为零的那条直线上的任意一点，也就是前面找到的那条直线。所有的解彼此之间只在被抹掉的方向上有差别。图 7 把两种情况放在了同一幅图里。













图 7: 多个输入，同一个输出。 直线 \((0,0,-1)+t(1,1,1)\) 上的五个输入，用空心圆标出。点击“播放”：\(C\) 把它们全都送到 \(\vec{b}=(1,0,-1)\)，而 \(\vec{b}'=(0,1,1)\) 没有任何输入能到达；从 \(\vec{b}'\) 落到平面的虚线表明它在平面之外。切换到 \(A\)：同样的五个输入被送到五个不同的输出。



这就解释了为什么矩阵 \(C\) 不可逆。
一个维度的信息丢失了。即使知道输出，我们也无法唯一地确定原来的输入。
从这个角度看，线性相关、秩和可逆性是紧密相连的。它们描述的是同一个根本问题的不同侧面。
线性相关告诉我们，矩阵的列向量里是否包含多余的方向。
秩告诉我们，这些列向量能张成多少维。
可逆性告诉我们，能否从变换的输出唯一地还原出原来的输入。
对于一个 \(3\times3\) 矩阵，如果它的三个列向量线性无关，那么它的秩是 3，矩阵可逆。
如果三个列向量线性相关，那么它的秩小于 3，矩阵不可逆。
我们还可以用行列式来判断一个方阵是否可逆：
\[
\det(A)\neq0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
A\text{ 可逆}
\]
如果
\[
\det(A)=0
\]
那么这个矩阵没有通常意义上的逆。
对于我们的两个例子，\(\det(A)=1\)（三角矩阵的行列式等于对角元的乘积），而 \(\det(C)=0\)。
事实上，对于可逆方阵，我们有：
\[
A^{-1}=\frac{\operatorname{adj}(A)}{\det(A)}
\]
其中 \(\operatorname{adj}(A)\) 是伴随矩阵。
如果行列式为零，这个公式的分母就是零，所以无法用这个式子求出逆矩阵。
但不可逆更深层的几何原因，正是我们前面讨论过的：变换把不同的输入映射到同一个输出，因此无法唯一地还原出原来的输入。
行列式也符合这幅图景。正如注 2 所说，行列式是一个变换对体积的缩放倍数。\(C\) 把整个三维空间压扁到一个平面上，而任何扁平的东西体积都是零，所以 \(\det(C)\) 必然为零。行列式为零并不是一条单独的规则，它就是同一次坍缩，只不过是用体积来衡量。在 图 3 里可以亲眼看到这一点：当两列逐渐对齐时，阴影平行四边形越来越细，面积趋于零。
这是我重新学习线性代数时慢慢意识到的。
许多起初看起来毫不相关的概念，比如矩阵、线性组合、线性相关、秩、行列式和逆矩阵，其实都可以从线性变换这个统一的几何视角来理解。
当我们不再只关注怎样计算公式，而是试着去理解在变换中向量和整个空间发生了什么时，这些概念之间的联系就清楚多了。

title: 解线性方程组
text:
本文译自英文原文 Solving Linear Equations，如有出入，以英文版为准。
在上一篇里，我从向量和线性变换的角度看矩阵。这一次换一个角度：线性方程组。我最感兴趣的，是解方程组背后的几何意义，以及高斯消元如何自然地引出 LU 分解。

title: 解线性方程组
section: 1 直线、平面和它们的法向量
text:
1 直线、平面和它们的法向量
考虑两个未知数的两个方程：
\[
\begin{cases}
x-2y=1,\\
3x+2y=11.
\end{cases}
\]
每个方程描述平面上的一条直线，方程组的解就是两条直线的交点 \((x,y)=(3,1)\)（图 1）。写成矩阵形式，就是
\[
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\3&2\end{bmatrix}}_{A}
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\end{bmatrix}}_{\vec{x}}
=
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1\\11\end{bmatrix}}_{\vec{b}}
\]






  
  
  
  
  
  
  n1
  n2


  One point
  No solution
  Infinitely many







图 1: 两个方程，两条直线。 每个方程是一条直线，解就是它们的交点。箭头是法向量 \(\vec{n}_1=(1,-2)\) 和 \(\vec{n}_2=(3,2)\)，按三分之一的长度画出。按钮把第二条直线换成法向量为 \(2\vec{n}_1\) 的直线：要么是一条平行线，无解；要么是同一条直线，有无穷多解。



三个未知数的三个方程，每个方程描述空间中的一个平面，解就是三个平面的公共点。例如
\[
\begin{cases}
x+y+z=4,\\
x-y+z=2,\\
2x-z=0
\end{cases}
\]
的解是 \((x,y,z)=(1,1,2)\)（图 2）。几何对象从直线变成了平面，代数形式仍然是 \(A\vec{x}=\vec{b}\)。













图 2: 三个方程，三个平面。 每两个平面交于一条直线（深色），三条交线都经过解 \((1,1,2)\)。按钮把第三个平面换成法向量为另外两个法向量之和的平面，\(\vec{n}_3=\vec{n}_1+\vec{n}_2\)：取决于它的右端，三个平面要么没有公共点，要么共用一整条直线。拖动图形可以从另一侧观察。



直线或平面是否交于一点，取决于它们的倾斜方向，而平面的倾斜方向由它的法向量描述，这是我在高中几何里学过的。平面 \(ax+by+cz=d\) 的法向量是 \(\vec{n}=(a,b,c)\)，前提是 \((a,b,c)\ne(0,0,0)\)。为什么？在平面上任取两点 \(P_1=(x_1,y_1,z_1)\) 和 \(P_2=(x_2,y_2,z_2)\)。它们都满足平面方程，两式相减，用点积的语言写出来就是
\[
(a,b,c)\cdot(x_1-x_2,\ y_1-y_2,\ z_1-z_2)=0
\]
第二个向量沿着平面的方向。既然对平面上任意两点都成立，\((a,b,c)\) 就垂直于平面内的每一个方向，这正是法向量的含义。同样，直线 \(ax+by=c\) 的法向量是 \((a,b)\)。
法向量告诉我们什么时候有唯一解。在二维中，法向量线性无关，两条直线就不平行，交于一点；法向量线性相关，两条直线就平行或重合，要么无解，要么有无穷多解。在三维中，三个法向量线性无关，三个平面就恰好交于一点。如果法向量张成的方向少于三个，就不可能有唯一解，方程组要么无解，要么有无穷多解，取决于这些方程是否相容。用矩阵的语言说，独立法向量的个数就是 \(A\) 的秩。

title: 解线性方程组
section: 2 消元在几何上做了什么
text:
2 消元在几何上做了什么
解方程组时，我们通常不断消去变量，直到方程组变成上三角形式。我觉得更有意思的是去问：每一步在几何上意味着什么？
回到那两条直线，把第二个方程替换为第二个方程减去第一个方程的三倍：
\[
(3x+2y)-3(x-2y)=11-3
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
8y=8
\]
新的直线 \(y=1\) 和原来的第二条直线不同，但它仍然经过 \((3,1)\)。解没有变，是因为这一步可以撤销：把第一个方程的三倍加回去，就得到原来的第二个方程。
法向量也按同样的方式变化：
\[
\vec{n}_2'=\vec{n}_2-3\vec{n}_1=(3,2)-3(1,-2)=(0,8)
\]
所以，从一个方程中减去另一个方程的倍数，就是让第二条直线绕着固定的交点旋转（图 3）。消元选的倍数，恰好让 \(\vec{n}_2'\) 竖直向上：直线变成水平的，\(x\) 从方程里消失，可以直接读出 \(y=1\)。

图 3: 消元让直线绕着解旋转。 第二个方程被替换为它自己减去第一个方程的 \(\ell\) 倍。第二条直线绕着 \((3,1)\) 转动，它的法向量从 \(\vec{n}_2\) 变成 \(\vec{n}_2-\ell\vec{n}_1\)；点线段就是 \(-\ell\vec{n}_1\) 这一步，法向量同样按三分之一的长度画出。拖动滑块，或者点「消去 x」到 \(\ell=3\)，这时直线变成 \(y=1\)。



在三维中也是一样。把一个平面的方程换成两个方程的组合，这个平面变了，但两个平面的交线保持不变。消元不断这样转动平面（图 4），直到方程组变成上三角形式：最后一个平面是水平的，它上面那个平面的方程里没有 \(x\)，于是可以依次读出 \(z\)、\(y\)、\(x\)。














图 4: 三维中的消元。 对 图 2 中的三个平面一步一步地消元。每一步从一个方程中减去另一个方程的倍数，所以变化的平面绕着它和另一个平面的交线（粗线）转动，三个平面始终经过 \((1,1,2)\)。第 3 步之后，方程组变成上三角形式：\(x+y+z=4\)、\(-2y=-2\)、\(-3z=-6\)。拖动图形可以从另一侧观察。

title: 解线性方程组
text:
3 把消元记录下来：\(PA=LU\)
高斯消元把 \(A\) 变成上三角矩阵 \(U\)。与其把它当作一次性的计算，我们可以把得到 \(U\) 的那些操作记录下来。在两条直线的例子里，从第二行减去第一行的三倍，这个操作本身就是一个矩阵：
\[
E=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\-3&1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
EA=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\0&8\end{bmatrix}=U
\]
撤销这一步，得到 \(A=E^{-1}U\)：
\[
A=
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\3&1\end{bmatrix}}_{L}
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\0&8\end{bmatrix}}_{U}
\]
这就是 LU 分解。\(U\) 是消元的结果，下三角矩阵 \(L\) 以能还原出 \(A\) 的形式保存了乘数 \(3\)。
步骤不止一步时，需要知道逆矩阵的一个性质。对于方阵 \(A\)，如果它的逆 \(A^{-1}\) 存在，就满足 \(A^{-1}A=AA^{-1}=I\)，而乘积的逆要把顺序反过来：
\[
(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}
\]
如果把矩阵看作依次进行的变换，这就说得通了：\(AB\) 先做 \(B\) 再做 \(A\)，所以要撤销它，就要先撤销 \(A\)，再撤销 \(B\)。
上面三个平面的例子需要三步：从第 2 行减去第 1 行的 \(1\) 倍（\(E_{21}\)），从第 3 行减去第 1 行的 \(2\) 倍（\(E_{31}\)），再从第 3 行减去新的第 2 行的 \(1\) 倍（\(E_{32}\)）：
\[
E_{32}E_{31}E_{21}A=U=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&1\\0&-2&0\\0&0&-3\end{bmatrix}
\]
按相反的顺序撤销这三步，
\[
A=E_{21}^{-1}E_{31}^{-1}E_{32}^{-1}U=
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\1&1&0\\2&1&1\end{bmatrix}}_{L}U
\]
\(L\) 存着三个乘数 \(1\)、\(2\) 和 \(1\)，每一个都在它所消去的那个元素的位置上。正是相反的顺序让它们保持干净。正向的乘积 \(E_{32}E_{31}E_{21}\) 左下角是 \(-1\)，而不是 \(-2\)：它用第 2 行去改第 3 行时，第 2 行已经被改过了，所以乘数混在了一起。而按相反顺序相乘，这些逆矩阵只是把每个乘数放到各自的位置上。
为什么要保留 \(L\)？假设 \(A\) 不变，而我们要对很多个右端 \(\vec{b}\) 求解 \(A\vec{x}=\vec{b}\)。有了 \(A=LU\)，每个新的 \(\vec{b}\) 只需要解两个三角方程组，
\[
L\vec{y}=\vec{b},\qquad U\vec{x}=\vec{y}
\]
用前代和回代即可。我们也可以保存行变换本身，再对每个新的 \(\vec{b}\) 重放一遍。LU 正是做这件事的一种有结构的方式。 节省是很可观的：对 \(n\times n\) 矩阵消元大约需要 \(n^3/3\) 次乘法，而两个三角方程组只需要大约 \(n^2\) 次。
还剩一个麻烦：并不是每个可逆矩阵都能在不交换行的情况下这样分解。例如，
\[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}
\]
是可逆的，但它的第一个主元是零，必须先交换两行。置换矩阵 \(P\) 记录这些行交换，于是得到一般的形式
\[
PA=LU
\]
用它求解 \(A\vec{x}=\vec{b}\) 时，右端也要做同样的置换：\(LU\vec{x}=P\vec{b}\)。
对我来说，最主要的想法是：LU 并不是独立于高斯消元的另一个技巧。它就是消元已经做过的工作，被记录下来，以便重复使用。

title: 解线性方程组
text:
4 转置，暂且如此
转置 \(A^T\) 交换 \(A\) 的行和列；我把它想象成矩阵的元素沿主对角线翻折过去。满足 \(A=A^T\) 的矩阵叫对称矩阵。和逆矩阵一样，乘积的转置也要把顺序反过来，\((AB)^T=B^TA^T\)。我可以从定义验证这一点，但转置、点积和正交之间的联系，等以后再看会更有意思，所以这里先不展开。1
1 更新（2026-10-29）： 这个联系在下一篇里出现了。点积可以用转置写成 \(\vec{x}\cdot\vec{y}=\vec{x}^T\vec{y}\)，所以 \(A^T\vec{e}\) 一次给出了 \(\vec{e}\) 与 \(A\) 每一列的点积。最小二乘要求误差垂直于每一列，即 \(A^T(\vec{y}-A\hat{\vec{w}})=\vec{0}\)，由此得到正规方程。见《向量空间与最小二乘》。现在，我想从这一篇里留下的两个想法是：消元的几何意义，以及 LU 如何把它记录下来。
